newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Land acquisition seen key to Hang Lung.
newsitem.headline: Land acquisition seen key to Hang Lung.

text.p: Hong Kong property firm Hang Lung Development Co has talked about buying new land for over a year, but analysts want to see more action.
"When you are too conservative and buy no land, you have no new projects and so your earnings prospects will start getting more and more difficult," said an analyst with a European house.
The market may soon get its wish. In a recent interview Hang Lung chairman Ronnie Chan said the firm was likely to spend HK$6 billion ($770 million) to buy land in calendar 1997.
In particular, he's keeping an eye on every project for tender associated with the development of a railway link to the territory's new airport now under construction.
But some analysts say the company has not been aggressive enough. Hang Lung has made no purchases at government land auctions since March 1995.
Its 55.1-percent-held subsidiary Amoy Properties Ltd has not walked away with anything from the auctions -- a major channel for developers to buy large sites -- for more than a year.
"It is not aggressive in buying land and is not buying enough," said Nicholas Wong, property analyst at HSBC James Capel.

"Last year, land prices hit rock-bottom but it didn't buy enough. That affects its growth," Wong added. "Now prices have rebounded and are not as cheap any more. In hindsight, it's been too conservative."

Despite continued talk of future land purchases, Hang Lung's shares have languished over the past 12 months, edging up a mere 2.2 percent compared with a far more robust 19.0 percent leap in Hong Kong's benchmark Hang Seng index.
Hang Lung Development last traded at HK$15.95 on Wednesday before market holidays on Thursday and Friday.

Analysts, however, remain cautiously optimistic about the profit growth potential in 1996/97 (July-June) for both Hang Lung Development, which develops properties mainly for sale, and Amoy, which develops investment properties.

They expect Hang Lung Development's net profit to edge up six percent to HK$2.41 billion and Amoy's net to climb nine percent to HK$1.72 billion in 1996/97, according to a survey of broker forecasts compiled by Edinburgh Financial Publishing.
Chan said 1996/97 results should be buoyed by Hang Lung's sale of residential flats and rental revenue from Amoy, which usually contributes 40-60 percent of the parent's net profit.

"There is rental growth (at Amoy), but not very big," Chan said, adding some of the focus would shift to selling non-core holdings such as less prominent offices and car parks. "This year we will try our best to sell the marginal properties."
One analyst said such sales at Amoy could bolster earnings and that the goal appeared tangible given Hong Kong's buoyant property market conditions.
Hang Lung Development would also benefit from strength at subsidiary Grand Hotel Holdings Ltd in 1996/97 due to the local hotel industry's improving environment, Chan said.

Looking ahead, analysts said they saw further but modest growth in 1997/98 net profits for Hang Lung and Amoy. They predicted the parent would book a net profit of HK$2.54 billion and Amoy HK$1.78 billion.
Chan said Hang Lung Development was "not pessimistic" about 1997/98 although the year might see smaller revenues.
"Most of the flats that are to be sold will have been sold in 1996/97," he said. "There will be fewer sales in 1997/98."
Hang Lung Development's landbank stands at about 2.5 million to three million square feet in Hong Kong, while Amoy has a land bank of about seven million square feet in Hong Kong, Chan said.
